vignette: Michael, a 34-year-old European-American married man and a dedicated firefighter, has been struggling with PTSD symptoms following his deployment as a relief worker in a war zone. The trauma he experienced there has profoundly affected his daily life, leaving him feeling perpetually on guard. The traumatic event that triggered Michael's current struggles occurred during a mission where the compound they were operating out of came under heavy gunfire. Despite their best efforts to secure the area and provide aid, several civilians were injured, and the chaos and violence left an indelible mark on Michael’s psyche. He vividly remembers the cacophony of gunshots, the smell of smoke, and the sight of frightened faces, all of which have become potent triggers for his current symptoms. Since returning from the war zone, Michael has adopted several maladaptive strategies to cope with the overwhelming feelings of threat he experiences daily. One such strategy is avoiding exercise, as the exertion often leaves him feeling vulnerable and exposed. He also tries to stay near exits wherever he goes, ensuring that he can quickly leave if necessary. Additionally, he pushes away positive emotions because they feel unsafe to him; the sudden shift from a calm state to heightened alertness triggered by these emotions makes him anxious. These maladaptive strategies have contributed significantly to his sense of threat. For instance, Michael feels on guard even inside his own home, constantly scanning for exits as soon as he enters any room or building. This hyper-vigilance is exacerbated when strangers approach him in ordinary situations; he perceives them as potential threats and becomes increasingly anxious. His occupation as a firefighter has also been affected by these symptoms. Michael finds himself avoiding physical training sessions at work because they remind him of the sense of vulnerability he felt during the war zone deployment. This avoidance, however, has led to a decrease in his overall fitness level, which affects his performance on the job and adds to his stress. Michael's marriage has also suffered due to these symptoms. He often avoids spending time with his family because even familiar environments now feel unsafe. His wife has noticed that he becomes agitated when they engage in activities that require leaving their home, such as going out for dinner or attending social events. This avoidance has led to increased tension and a sense of isolation between them. Michael’s maladaptive strategies have created a cycle where his attempts to manage his anxiety only reinforce his sense of threat. For example, the more he avoids positive emotions, the more isolated he feels from others, which in turn heightens his perception of danger. His constant need to stay near exits and avoid exercise keeps him on edge, further cementing his belief that threats are omnipresent. What frightens Michael most is the feeling that he will never be able to fully trust his environment again. He has come to believe that safety is an illusion and that danger can strike at any moment. This pervasive sense of threat makes it challenging for him to engage in daily activities without feeling constantly vigilant and anxious. Despite these challenges, what brings Michael to seek help now is a growing realization that his symptoms are affecting not only his work but also his relationships. He hopes that with the right support, he can regain some semblance of normalcy and find ways to cope more effectively with his trauma without relying on maladaptive strategies.
